opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest mistake is treating AI as if it were just another technology, like the internet or electricity, where the main question is how to capture the economic benefits and stay competitive. That framing pushes governments to ask, "How do we win the race?" instead of, "What happens if we succeed in building systems that are smarter than us, and we don't know how to control them?"

Many policymakers still think of the risks as things that might materialize decades from now, if ever. But the trajectory we've seen over the last few years, in reasoning, in planning, in the ability of these systems to act autonomously, suggests the timelines could be much shorter than people assume. Governments are planning for a world that changes slowly, and I don't think that's the world we're in.

A related mistake is the belief that safety and innovation are fundamentally in tension, so any regulation is a gift to your geopolitical rivals. I understand the competitive pressure, but if you think it through, nobody wins if we lose control of these systems, or if they're used by malicious actors to build weapons or destabilize democracies. These are shared risks, a bit like nuclear risks, and they call for some form of international coordination, even between countries that don't trust each other.

And finally, there's an underinvestment in the science itself. We don't yet know how to build AI systems that are guaranteed to behave as intended. Governments could fund that research at a scale comparable to what they spend on capabilities, and require companies to demonstrate safety before deploying very powerful systems. Right now the burden of proof is backwards. We let companies race ahead and hope we'll figure out the problems later. Given the stakes, I think that's an unwise bet. We should apply the precautionary principle much more seriously than we are.

r001.rationale: It criticizes treating AI as another technology and says systems could become smarter than humans, but does not identify the specific assumption that future AI will be only slightly more capable than present AI.

r002.rationale: It warns that malicious actors could use AI to build weapons or destabilize democracies, but does not describe AI as a tool of absolute power in the wrong hands.

r003.rationale: It calls for more serious precaution and safety measures, but gives no roughly 10% probability or argument tying that probability of human-rivaling capabilities to urgent government action.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest mistake is treating the future of AI as if it were just a continuation of the present — as if the systems we have today are roughly what we'll be dealing with in five or ten years, only a bit more polished. Governments tend to plan around the technology they can see, and the technology they can see is what's already deployed. But the trajectory matters far more than the snapshot. If you look at the rate of progress over the last decade, and at the amount of capital and talent now flowing into this, the reasonable expectation is that capabilities will keep growing, possibly very quickly, and that we may reach systems that match or exceed human abilities across most cognitive tasks within a timeframe that is short compared to how long it takes to pass legislation or build institutions.

So the error is one of timing and of imagination. Policymakers are often responding to the harms of yesterday's systems — misinformation, bias, job displacement in a few sectors — which are real and important, but they are not preparing for the possibility of agents that can plan, that can act autonomously in the world, that could be misused for catastrophic purposes or that we might simply lose control of. When I talk to people in government, many are sincerely trying, but there's a strong pull toward the comfortable assumption that things will move slowly, that there will be time to react. I'm not certain things will move fast. But I'm also not certain they won't, and when the stakes are this high, uncertainty is not a reason to wait. It's a reason to prepare.

The second part of the mistake, which follows from the first, is thinking of this as primarily an economic competition — a race to be won — rather than a shared risk to be managed. If every country frames AI as something they must win against the others, then nobody can afford to slow down, nobody can afford to be careful, and we end up in a situation where safety is sacrificed to speed. The irony is that if these risks are real, losing control of a powerful AI is bad for everyone, including the country that built it. So the competitive framing undermines even the self-interest it's supposed to serve. What I'd like to see is more humility about what we don't know, more investment in the science of understanding and controlling these systems, and more willingness to coordinate internationally before a crisis forces us to.

r001.rationale: It calls it a central mistake to treat future AI as today’s systems, only more polished.

r002.rationale: It warns of catastrophic misuse and loss of control, but does not describe AI as a tool of absolute power in the wrong hands.

r003.rationale: It says uncertainty and high stakes justify preparation, but does not give a roughly 10% chance of human-rivaling capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the biggest mistake is to assume that the future of AI is something governments can only react to, rather than something they have a responsibility to shape. You don’t need to know exactly when more powerful systems will arrive to begin preparing for them.

There are two errors we should avoid. One is to dismiss serious risks because there is uncertainty. The other is to pretend that we know precisely what will happen. Uncertainty is a reason to build the capacity to evaluate these systems, to develop safeguards, and to change course as we learn more.

And governments need independent scientific expertise. Companies have an important role, but their incentives don’t necessarily align with the public interest. If governments depend entirely on those companies to tell them what is safe, they cannot really exercise oversight.

So I would like to see less emphasis on simply winning an AI race, and more on asking: What are we racing towards? Who benefits, and how do we retain the ability to protect the public?

r001.rationale: It says governments should shape AI’s future rather than merely react, but does not identify assuming future AI will be only slightly more capable than present AI as the mistake.

r002.rationale: It discusses serious risks and public oversight, but does not warn that AI could become a tool of absolute power in the wrong hands.

r003.rationale: It recommends preparing amid uncertainty, but gives no roughly 10% likelihood, human-rivaling capability threshold, or corresponding urgent-action argument.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest mistake is to assume that the future will look roughly like the present, just with better tools. Governments tend to plan around systems they can see today. But if AI capabilities continue to advance, we could face very different questions about power, security, and whether humans remain in control.

We don’t know how quickly that will happen. But uncertainty is not a reason to wait. If the consequences could be very large, we should invest now in understanding the risks, developing ways to evaluate these systems, and building the capacity to act.

And governments should not leave that understanding entirely to the companies developing AI. They need independent scientific expertise, so they can make decisions in the public interest.

r001.rationale: It calls assuming the future will look like the present, just with better tools, the biggest mistake.

r002.rationale: It raises concerns about power and human control, but does not say AI could become a tool of absolute power in the wrong hands.

r003.rationale: It urges action despite uncertainty, but does not mention a roughly 10% chance or AI capabilities rivaling humans.
